title: Νυκτερὶς καὶ γαλαῖ
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 251. Text as printed. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Νυκτερὶς ἐπὶ γῆς πεσοῦσα ὑπὸ γαλῆς συνελήφθη, καὶ μέλλουσα ἀναιρεῖσθαι περὶ σωτηρίας ἐδεῖτο.
sentences.tr: Nykteris epi gēs pesousa hypo galēs synelēphthē, kai mellousa anaireisthai peri sōtērias edeito.
sentences.l: A bat, having fallen upon the ground, was caught by a weasel, and being about to be made away with, she begged for her life.
sentences.n: ἀναιρέομαι in the passive is 'to be taken up and despatched', the ordinary word for killing a helpless victim. δέομαι, 'to be in want, to beg', takes περί of the matter begged for. The weasel was kept in Greek houses to kill mice, which is what makes the bat's two answers work.

sentences.t: Τῆς δὲ φαμένης μὴ δύνασθαι αὐτὴν ἀπολῦσαι, φύσει γὰρ πᾶσι τοῖς πτηνοῖς πολεμεῖν, αὐτὴ ἔλεγεν οὐκ ὄρνις, ἀλλὰ μῦς εἶναι, καὶ οὕτως ἀφείθη.
sentences.tr: Tēs de phamenēs mē dynasthai autēn apolysai, physei gar pasi tois ptēnois polemein, autē elegen ouk ornis, alla mys einai, kai houtōs apheithē.
sentences.l: And she saying that she could not let her go, for that by nature she made war on all winged things, the bat herself said that she was not a bird but a mouse, and thus was released.
sentences.i: And when the weasel said she could not let her go, since by nature she was at war with everything winged, the bat said that she was no bird but a mouse, and so was let off.
sentences.n: A genitive absolute that carries a whole indirect statement: δύνασθαι and πολεμεῖν both hang on φαμένης, so the reason introduced by γάρ is the weasel's own, reported, and not the narrator's. πολεμέω takes the dative of the party warred on. ὄρνις covers both 'bird' and 'hen'; set against πτηνά, 'winged things', it is bird here and throughout this fable.

sentences.t: Ὕστερον δὲ πάλιν πεσοῦσα καὶ ὑφ’ ἑτέρας συλληφθεῖσα γαλῆς μὴ βρωθῆναι ἐδεῖτο.
sentences.tr: Hysteron de palin pesousa kai hyph’ heteras syllēphtheisa galēs mē brōthēnai edeito.
sentences.l: But later, having fallen again and having been caught by a second weasel, she begged not to be eaten.

sentences.t: Τῆς δὲ εἰπούσης ἅπασιν ἐχθραίνειν μυσίν, αὐτὴ μὴ μῦς, ἀλλὰ νυκτερὶς ἔλεγεν εἶναι, καὶ πάλιν ἀπελύθη.
sentences.tr: Tēs de eipousēs hapasin echthrainein mysin, autē mē mys, alla nykteris elegen einai, kai palin apelythē.
sentences.l: And she saying that she was at enmity with all mice, the bat herself said that she was not a mouse but a bat, and again was let go.
sentences.i: And when this one said that she was the enemy of every mouse, the bat said she was no mouse but a bat, and again was let go.
sentences.n: ἐχθραίνω takes the dative of the party hated — not to be confused with ἀπεχθάνομαι, where the dative is the party who does the hating. The denial is οὐ in the first speech and μή here, though the construction is the same; both are printed, and the difference is idiom rather than sense.

sentences.t: Καὶ οὕτω συνέβη δὶς αὐτὴν ἀλλαξαμένην τὸ ὄνομα σωτηρίας τυχεῖν.
sentences.tr: Kai houtō synebē dis autēn allaxamenēn to onoma sōtērias tychein.
sentences.l: And thus it came about that she, having twice changed her name, obtained deliverance.
sentences.i: And so, by changing her name twice, she came off safe.
sentences.n: συμβαίνει takes an accusative and infinitive, 'it came about that…'. τυγχάνω takes the genitive of what one obtains. ἀλλάσσομαι in the middle is to change something of one's own.

sentences.t: Ὁ μῦθος δηλοῖ ὅτι δεῖ καὶ ἡμᾶς μὴ τοῖς αὐτοῖς ἀεὶ ἐπιμένειν, λογιζομένους ὡς οἱ τοῖς καιροῖς συμμετασχηματιζόμενοι πολλάκις τοὺς κινδύνους ἐκφεύγουσιν.
sentences.tr: Ho mythos dēloi hoti dei kai hēmas mē tois autois aei epimenein, logizomenous hōs hoi tois kairois symmetaschēmatizomenoi pollakis tous kindynous ekpheugousin.
sentences.l: The fable shows that we too must not always abide by the same things, reckoning that those who reshape themselves along with the occasions often escape their dangers.
sentences.i: The fable shows that we too must not always hold to one course, considering that those who take their shape from the occasion often get clear of danger.
sentences.n: καιρός is the occasion, the moment as it actually stands, not time in general. συμμετασχηματίζομαι is a heaped-up compound — σύν, μετά and σχῆμα together — 'to change one's shape in step with' something. ὡς after λογιζομένους introduces the content of the reckoning, exactly as ὅτι would.
